line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 f3
teaches: A modest pawn move that props up the centre is often also the first move of a pawn storm — ask what it enables as well as what it defends, and what square it takes away from your own pieces.
explains: The pawn to f3 does two jobs. It puts a second guard on e4, which the bishop on g7 has been staring at down the long diagonal since it came out, and it prepares to push the g-pawn and roll the kingside pawns at the castled king. The cost is real and permanent: the knight on g1 can no longer come to f3, so it has to take the slower route through e2.

line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 e4 d6 f3 O-O
teaches: Castle before choosing a plan when several plans are all playable — the king move is common to all of them, so it costs nothing and buys a move of information about what the opponent commits to.
explains: Black castles, which is automatic here — every reasonable system against this setup starts the same way. The choice comes next, and there are three: the flank break with the c-pawn two squares, which is the line reckoned objectively best; the queenside expansion with the knight to c6, then the a-pawn, the rook, and the b-pawn; and the old central strike with the e-pawn, which is the traditional way to play this defence and is perfectly viable despite its reputation. White, meanwhile, will develop the dark-squared bishop or bring the knight round to e2, and those two often transpose into one another.
